title: Maya and the veil (7.20–7.30)
hook: Krishna says he is hidden in plain sight, covered by his own maya

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnani: four kinds of devotees, the one in distress, the curious, the one who asks, and the one who knows, all four noble. Today, the last day of chapter seven.

Watch a great magic show up close. The magician is right there, three feet away, sleeves rolled up. Nothing's hidden. And you still can't see how it's done. The trick isn't that the magician is behind a curtain. It's that you're looking exactly where the magician wants you to look. There's a Sanskrit word for a power like that: maya. It's often translated as illusion. But in the Gita, Krishna uses it about himself. He says he's right here, and hidden, covered by his own maya.
screen: `THREE FEET AWAY. NOTHING HIDDEN.` → `STILL YOU CAN'T SEE IT.` → `MAYA.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-five: I am not revealed to everyone, veiled by my yoga-maya. This confused world doesn't recognize me, unborn and unchanging. Hindu schools read the word differently. In Advaita Vedanta, maya is the power by which the one reality appears as many; the world isn't ultimately what it seems. In devotional schools like those of Ramanuja and Madhva, the world is real, and maya is the Lord's real power, which can both reveal and hide. Either way, the veil is his. Around it, these verses say something generous and something hard. Generous, verses twenty-one and twenty-two: whatever form a devotee wants to worship with faith, I make that faith steady, and what they receive, they receive from me. Hard, verse twenty-four: people who don't understand think the unseen has simply become something seen, without knowing the higher, unchanging nature behind it. And verse twenty-seven names what does the veiling inside us: the pair of wanting and not-wanting. From birth, everyone is caught in that push and pull. Those who come out of it, verse twenty-eight says, worship steadily. And the chapter ends by naming words the next chapter will explain: Brahman, the self, action, and more. What's behind the veil isn't far away. It's covered.
screen: `HIDDEN BY MY OWN MAYA.` · `SCHOOLS READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · `WHATEVER FORM, I MAKE FAITH STEADY.` · `THE VEIL OF WANTING AND NOT-WANTING.` · then, large: `NOT FAR. COVERED.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-seven says the veil is woven of liking and disliking, so watch the weaving: each time something comes up, a sound, a memory, an itch, label it silently, like or dislike, and don't change anything. After a while, see if there's a moment between the like and the dislike, a thin gap where nothing's being pulled. Rest there.
Maya. Illusion, Krishna's own power, which hides him in plain sight. The veil is woven from wanting and not-wanting.
Your line: behind the veil. Liking and disliking do the weaving. That's chapter seven, complete.

howItsDone: Hindu schools understand maya in different ways: Advaita Vedanta teaches it as the appearance of the one reality as many, while Vaishnava schools teach it as the Lord's real power; many Hindus speak of maya when describing the pull of worldly wanting.

original.note: Sanskrit: maya, often translated illusion; in the Gita, Krishna's own power that veils him.

trapdoor: what you thought: maya means the world is fake.
what it means: Krishna's own power, which hides him in plain sight; inside us, woven from wanting and not-wanting.

what a scholar hears: in the Rig Veda maya is a god's power to make forms; Shankara's Advaita reads it as the appearance of Brahman as many, while Ramanuja rejects world-illusion and reads maya as the Lord's real, wondrous power.

7.20 and 7.23 speak of people who, their knowledge taken by desires, worship 'other gods' and receive finite fruit. The script leaves that framing out and uses 7.21–22 (Krishna steadies whatever faith). A Keeper should decide whether 7.20/7.23 need their own treatment.
